title: Bash: top client IPs in an access log
prompt:
Implement `summarize.sh` (it is currently a stub that exits 1): a script that reports the busiest clients in a web server access log.

Usage: `bash summarize.sh <logfile> [N]`

The log is in Apache/nginx common or combined log format, one request per line, for example
`203.0.113.7 - - [10/Oct/2023:13:55:36 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 2326`
(the combined format appends `"referer" "user-agent"` after the byte count). Sample logs are in `logs/`.

Visible tests (a partial set): `bash tests/run_tests.sh`

Specification:
- Output: the top N client IPs by request count, one per line, formatted exactly `<count> <ip>` (the count, one space, the ip; no leading or trailing whitespace, no padding). Sort by count descending (numerically), ties broken by ip ascending using plain string comparison (byte order, so `10.0.0.10` sorts before `10.0.0.2`, and `10.0.0.2` before `9.9.9.9`). N is a positive integer and defaults to 3. If there are fewer than N distinct IPs, print what exists. An empty file, or a file with no countable lines, prints nothing and exits 0.
- Which lines count:
  - The line must start with an IPv4 address immediately followed by a space: four dot-separated groups of one to three digits (a shape check only, no range check). Every other line is ignored: leading whitespace, IPv6, hostnames, blank lines, garbage.
  - The HTTP status is the first token after the closing quote of the first double-quoted string on the line (the request, which may contain spaces but never a double quote). The line counts only if that status is exactly three digits and starts with 2 or 3 (2xx or 3xx). A line with no such quoted request, or with any other status or token there, is ignored.
  - An IP none of whose lines count is not listed at all.
  - A final line without a trailing newline is still a line.
- Errors: if the log file does not exist, print `error: no such file: <path>` (the path exactly as given) to stderr, print nothing to stdout, and exit 2.
- Portability: it must run with the system `bash`, `awk` and `sort` on both macOS and Linux (macOS ships bash 3.2 and BSD tools), so avoid GNU-only options and bash-4-only features. File paths may contain spaces.
